## Introduction

Arthritis is a heterogeneous group of joint disorders characterized by persistent inflammation, pain, stiffness, and progressive damage to cartilage, bone, synovium, and periarticular connective tissues (Disease code: arthritis). In the analysis of the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project data, circulating levels of 315 plasma proteins were found to be significantly associated with arthritis, based on 36,678 controls and 934 cases, after applying Bonferroni correction at P < 1 × 10⁻⁹. Understanding the molecular mechanisms reflected by these 315 proteins is essential because arthritis arises from the coordinated action of immune activation, inflammatory signaling, extracellular matrix remodeling, leukocyte recruitment, and altered bone homeostasis, all of which contribute to clinical progression and structural joint injury.

To define this molecular landscape more systematically, we performed a comprehensive functional enrichment analysis on the 315 arthritis-associated proteins, screening biological pathways from multiple resources including Gene Ontology Molecular Function, Gene Ontology Biological Process, Gene Ontology Cellular Component, Reactome, and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes. After correction for multiple testing, we identified 103 significantly enriched biological pathways (Table 1). These pathways reveal a coherent and quantitatively supported disease framework dominated by cytokine-mediated inflammatory signaling, interleukin-linked communication, tumor necrosis factor receptor biology, neutrophil granule activity, antibody-associated immune processes, cell adhesion, extracellular matrix disassembly, matrix metalloproteinase activity, and osteoblast differentiation. The enrichment profile therefore indicates that arthritis-associated proteins are not randomly distributed across biological functions, but instead converge on interconnected processes involving innate immunity, adaptive immunity, tissue destruction, vascular and stromal interactions, and bone remodeling. In the following sections, we examine the most significant pathways and their associated protein networks in greater detail to clarify the molecular architecture underlying arthritis.

## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, the enriched biological pathways are ranked on the basis of statistical significance, biological coherence, and disease relevance. Taken together, the results consistently indicate inflammatory, immune, and tissue-remodeling mechanisms that are central to arthritis. Among the most statistically significant signals, signaling by interleukins (REAC:R-HSA-449147, p = 2.61 × 10−10, 39 associated proteins) and tumor necrosis factors bind their physiological receptors (REAC:R-HSA-5669034, p = 3.25 × 10−12, 13 associated proteins) stand out, alongside cytokines and inflammatory response (WP:WP530, p = 1.40 × 10−4, 7 associated proteins) and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells transcription factor binding motif enrichment (TF:M00194_1, p = 5.10 × 10−3, 21 associated proteins). These convergent enrichments are highly consistent with published evidence indicating that interleukins, tumor necrosis factor signaling, and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation contribute to synovial inflammation, leukocyte recruitment, and chronic joint damage in inflammatory arthritis, particularly rheumatoid arthritis.

Building on this inflammatory signaling framework, several additional enriched terms further support a substantial contribution from both innate immunity and adaptive immunity. The enrichment of specific granule (GO:0042581, p = 7.88 × 10−9, 18 associated proteins) suggests neutrophil activation, a process that has been well documented in inflamed synovial fluid and that may contribute to protease release, oxidative injury, and amplification of inflammation. In parallel, immunoglobulin complex (GO:0019814, p = 2.02 × 10−3, 4 associated proteins) points to antibody-mediated immune processes, which is in line with evidence that autoantibodies and immune complexes contribute to complement activation and persistent synovitis in autoimmune arthritis. Consistent with this interpretation, the direct enrichment of rheumatoid arthritis (KEGG:05323, p = 8.69 × 10−7, 14 associated proteins), arthritis (HP:0001369, p = 2.78 × 10−3, 17 associated proteins), and arthralgia (HP:0002829, p = 2.65 × 10−4, 17 associated proteins) further supports the disease relevance of this pathway set.

In addition to immune activation, the enrichment profile also points toward extracellular matrix injury and joint structural remodeling as major components of the observed disease biology. Extracellular matrix structural constituent (GO:0005201, p = 1.88 × 10−7, 17 associated proteins), extracellular matrix disassembly (GO:0022617, p = 1.53 × 10−6, 10 associated proteins), matrix metalloproteinases (WP:WP129, p = 2.45 × 10−4, 7 associated proteins), and cell adhesion molecules (KEGG:04514, p = 2.16 × 10−7, 19 associated proteins) collectively suggest active degradation of cartilage and connective tissue, together with enhanced leukocyte adhesion and migration into the joint. This overall pattern agrees with a large body of literature showing that matrix metalloproteinase-driven matrix breakdown and adhesion molecule-mediated immune cell infiltration are key mechanisms underlying pannus formation, cartilage erosion, and progressive joint destruction.

Extending this tissue-remodeling perspective, the enrichment of osteoblast differentiation (GO:0001649, p = 1.53 × 10−5, 14 associated proteins) may indicate altered bone remodeling, which is also a recognized feature of arthritis, where inflammatory mediators disrupt the balance between bone formation and bone resorption. Overall, the highly significant p-values across inflammatory signaling, neutrophil granule biology, antibody-associated immunity, extracellular matrix turnover, and bone differentiation support a model in which arthritis may be shaped by coordinated cytokine-dependent immune activation and progressive destruction of joint tissue. This interpretation remains closely aligned with the current biomedical literature and provides a coherent framework for the more detailed pathway discussion that follows.

## Enriched Pathways Analysis

With this overall enrichment pattern in mind, the following sections provide a more detailed discussion of the top enriched pathways.


### Factor: NF-kappaB; motif: NGGGGAMTTTCCNN; match class: 1 (TF:M00194_1) 

Nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells is a central transcriptional regulatory pathway that controls the expression of many genes involved in inflammation, innate immune defense, adaptive immune activation, cell survival, tissue remodeling, and osteoclast differentiation. The pathway is typically activated by proinflammatory cytokines, pattern recognition receptor ligands, antigen receptor signaling, cellular stress, and damage-associated signals. In its inactive state, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells dimers are retained in the cytoplasm by inhibitor of kappa B proteins. Upon stimulation, inhibitor of kappa B kinase complexes phosphorylate inhibitor of kappa B proteins, leading to their degradation and allowing nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells to translocate into the nucleus, where it binds specific deoxyribonucleic acid motifs such as the reported nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells consensus sequence and induces transcription of target genes. These targets include tumor necrosis factor, interleukin 1, interleukin 6, chemokines, adhesion molecules, matrix-degrading enzymes, cyclooxygenase 2, inducible nitric oxide synthase, and factors that promote osteoclastogenesis. Taken together, this broad transcriptional program positions nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells as a master regulator linking inflammatory signaling to synovial activation, cartilage destruction, bone erosion, and persistence of chronic joint disease.

This general biological framework also provides a useful basis for interpreting the potential arthritis relevance of the present enrichment result. No relevant publications were provided in the input list, so a publication-specific synthesis cannot be performed. Nevertheless, based on established biological knowledge, the nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells pathway appears strongly related to arthritis because it integrates many of the inflammatory signals that drive synovial pathology and structural joint damage. In inflammatory arthritis, cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor and interleukin 1 activate nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells in synovial macrophages, fibroblast-like synoviocytes, endothelial cells, chondrocytes, and osteoclast precursors. This activation promotes production of additional cytokines and chemokines, thereby amplifying leukocyte recruitment and sustaining chronic synovitis. The same pathway also induces matrix metalloproteinases and other catabolic mediators that degrade cartilage extracellular matrix, while simultaneously supporting receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells ligand-dependent osteoclast differentiation and bone resorption, which contributes to erosive disease. In addition, persistent nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells signaling enhances survival and aggressive behavior of synovial stromal cells, favoring pannus formation and invasive tissue remodeling. Thus, this pathway may be viewed not merely as associated with arthritis, but as a mechanistic hub that connects inflammatory stimulation to the major pathological features of arthritis, including pain-associated inflammation, synovial hyperplasia, cartilage breakdown, and bone destruction. Because no source publications were supplied, these statements should be interpreted as a general pathway-based analysis rather than a citation-grounded review of the provided literature.

Against this biological background, the enrichment results offer additional support for the relevance of this pathway to arthritis-related processes. There were 21 arthritis-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells as a central transcriptional regulatory pathway controlling the expression of genes involved in inflammation, innate immune defense, adaptive immune activation, cell survival, tissue remodeling, and osteoclast differentiation. This enrichment is highly consistent with the pathological features of arthritis because the pathway mechanistically connects upstream inflammatory stimuli, including proinflammatory cytokines, pattern recognition receptor ligands, antigen receptor signaling, cellular stress, and damage-associated signals, to downstream transcriptional programs that promote synovial activation, cartilage degradation, bone erosion, and chronic disease persistence. At the molecular level, the pathway coordinates the induction of numerous arthritis-relevant mediators, including tumor necrosis factor, interleukin 1, interleukin 6, chemokines, adhesion molecules, matrix-degrading enzymes, cyclooxygenase 2, inducible nitric oxide synthase, and osteoclast-promoting factors, indicating that the 21 enriched proteins converge on a biologically central inflammatory axis with broad effects across immune activation, tissue destruction, and joint remodeling.

To complement this pathway-level interpretation, the network view below provides a visual summary of the relationships among the enriched proteins. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for these 21 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage can be accessed through the embedded link for interactive network exploration.

Building on this network-level overview, the following paragraphs introduce several of the significant proteins identified during the function enrichment analysis in a more detailed and connected manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

BST2 stands out as one of the most arthritis-relevant proteins in this list because it integrates antiviral defense, interferon biology, inflammatory signaling, and tissue-remodeling pathways. Type I interferon signatures are prominent in several inflammatory arthritides, particularly systemic autoimmune conditions with joint involvement, and BST2 is a canonical interferon-inducible molecule. Its ability to regulate plasmacytoid dendritic cell interferon responses through LILRA4/ILT7 suggests a plausible role in shaping chronic innate immune activation within inflamed synovial tissues. In parallel, the reported nuclear factor kappa-B-related activity links BST2 to one of the central transcriptional programs driving synovitis, cytokine production, and leukocyte recruitment. Its inhibition of MMP14-dependent proteolytic activity is also notable, because matrix metalloproteinases contribute directly to cartilage degradation, pannus invasion, and structural joint damage in arthritis. Collectively, BST2 appears important not merely as an antiviral factor, but as a multifunctional regulator positioned at the intersection of interferon-driven inflammation, stromal invasion, and tissue destruction, all of which are highly relevant to arthritis pathogenesis.[[1]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18200009) [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18342597) [[3]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19036818) [[4]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19879838) [[5]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019814) [[6]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20399176) [[7]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20419159) [[8]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20940320) [[9]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21529378) [[10]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22520941) [[11]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19179289) [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20686043) [[13]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20943977) [[14]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21621240) [[15]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26378163) [[16]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31199522) [[17]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22065321) [[18]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19564354) [[19]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26172439) [[20]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23028328) 

From this interferon-linked and tissue-remodeling context, the report next turns to proteins that may contribute more directly to leukocyte movement and vascular entry into inflamed joints. ADAM8 is highly relevant to arthritis because leukocyte extravasation is a fundamental step in the establishment and maintenance of synovial inflammation. In inflammatory arthritis, the influx of neutrophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes into the synovium and synovial fluid drives cytokine production, pannus formation, and progressive joint damage. A protein implicated in leukocyte transmigration across the vascular wall may therefore contribute directly to the cellular composition of the inflamed joint. Given that metalloprotease-disintegrin family members often regulate adhesion, migration, and proteolytic remodeling of the extracellular environment, ADAM8 may plausibly participate in the recruitment and retention of inflammatory cells in arthritic tissues. Even though no citation is provided in the source entry, the listed function makes ADAM8 a mechanistically compelling candidate in arthritis biology.

A closely related aspect of chronic synovitis is vascular remodeling, which provides the structural basis for sustained inflammatory cell recruitment and pannus support. EPHB4 is particularly interesting in the context of arthritis because angiogenesis, endothelial remodeling, and altered vascular permeability are hallmarks of chronically inflamed synovium. Expansion of the synovial microvasculature supports leukocyte influx, nutrient delivery to hyperplastic pannus, and persistence of inflammatory lesions. Through its central roles in blood vessel remodeling and endothelial cell behavior, EPHB4 may influence the vascular architecture that sustains synovitis. Its regulation of cell adhesion and migration is also relevant to stromal organization and immune cell trafficking within the joint. In rheumatoid arthritis and related disorders, pathways that coordinate endothelial activation and pathologic neovascularization are strongly linked to disease progression; thus, EPHB4 represents a plausible mediator of the vascular component of arthritis pathology.

Consistent with this vascular perspective, endothelial junctional regulation may also be important for determining how efficiently immune cells enter inflamed tissue. ESAM is noteworthy because endothelial junction integrity is a major determinant of leukocyte passage and vascular leak during joint inflammation. In arthritis, activated synovial endothelium becomes permissive to immune cell infiltration, and cytoskeletal-junctional remodeling is central to this process. By coupling actin fibers to endothelial cell junctions through AMOTL2 and CDH5, ESAM may regulate barrier function, endothelial shape, and transmigration routes for inflammatory cells. These properties are directly relevant to synovitis, where excessive trafficking of leukocytes from blood into the synovium is a defining pathogenic event. Therefore, ESAM may contribute to the microvascular changes that enable persistent inflammatory cell accumulation in arthritic joints.[[21]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24806444) 

Beyond vascular entry and endothelial regulation, cytokine receptor systems may further amplify local immune communication within the synovial compartment. IL15RA is among the strongest arthritis-related candidates in the list because interleukin 15 is a well-established proinflammatory cytokine implicated in synovial immune activation. Interleukin 15 supports survival and activation of T cells and innate immune cells, both of which contribute to chronic joint inflammation. The capacity of IL15RA to mediate both cis and trans presentation is especially important, as trans-presentation amplifies local immune communication within tissues such as the synovium. Its reported role in neutrophil SYK activation and phagocytosis is also highly relevant, since neutrophils are abundant in inflamed joints and are major effectors of tissue injury through protease release, reactive oxygen species generation, and cytokine amplification. Because SYK signaling itself is a recognized inflammatory pathway in arthritis, IL15RA links cytokine biology with effector-cell activation in a manner that is mechanistically meaningful for disease pathogenesis.[[22]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17947230) 

In addition to cytokine-driven immune activation, chronic arthritis also involves substantial tissue adaptation and extracellular matrix remodeling. CHI3L1 is highly relevant to arthritis because it combines two processes central to joint disease: tissue remodeling and immune regulation. Arthritis involves not only inflammatory cytokine production but also remodeling of cartilage, synovium, and extracellular matrix, and CHI3L1 is explicitly linked to adaptation to tissue injury and environmental stress. Its effects on dendritic cell accumulation and macrophage differentiation are particularly important, as these myeloid populations shape synovial inflammation, antigen presentation, and fibrotic or reparative responses. Although the description emphasizes T helper 2 and mucosal or pulmonary contexts, the broader biology of CHI3L1 strongly supports a role in chronic inflammatory tissue remodeling, which is a key feature of arthritis. This makes CHI3L1 a plausible marker and mediator of joint inflammation, especially in settings where macrophage activation and matrix turnover are prominent.

This connection between myeloid regulation and persistent inflammation also leads naturally to proteins that may influence antigen presentation and adaptive immune maintenance. CD83 is relevant to arthritis because antigen presentation and subsequent lymphocyte activation are central mechanisms in autoimmune and chronic inflammatory joint disease. Synovial dendritic cells, macrophages, and activated B cells can present antigen locally, sustaining T-cell responses that promote cytokine production, autoantibody generation, and tissue injury. A molecule involved in antigen presentation and post-activation cellular interactions may therefore influence the intensity and persistence of adaptive immune responses in the joint microenvironment. Although the source description is concise and lacks direct citation, CD83 stands out as a functionally important immune-regulatory protein with plausible relevance to autoimmune arthritis.

Extending this adaptive immune theme, costimulatory control of T-cell persistence may be another mechanism contributing to chronic synovitis. TNFRSF9 is of interest in arthritis because it regulates T-cell survival and effector fitness, processes that can contribute to chronic immune activation in inflamed joints. While the description emphasizes antiviral and antitumor immunity, the same costimulatory logic is relevant to autoimmune settings in which persistent T-cell activation sustains synovitis. Enhanced survival and metabolic competence of activated T cells may support prolonged cytokine production and interactions with synovial macrophages, fibroblasts, and B cells. Thus, TNFRSF9 may represent a pathway through which adaptive immune persistence is reinforced in arthritis, especially in T cell-driven disease subsets.

Whereas some enriched proteins may promote persistence of inflammatory cells, others may be relevant because they influence whether pathogenic stromal and immune populations are removed. TNFRSF10B is potentially relevant to arthritis because dysregulated apoptosis is a key feature of chronic synovial inflammation. In rheumatoid arthritis, resistance of synovial fibroblasts and some immune cell populations to apoptosis contributes to pannus persistence, invasive behavior, and prolonged cytokine production. A receptor that mediates TRAIL-induced apoptosis may therefore influence whether inflammatory or stromal cells are eliminated or retained within diseased joints. The mention of modulation by decoy receptors is especially important, as local expression of anti-apoptotic regulators could blunt death signaling and favor chronicity. Accordingly, TNFRSF10B may be mechanistically linked to the defective cell turnover that characterizes destructive arthritis.[[23]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10549288) [[24]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26457518) 

In parallel with cell survival control, angiogenesis remains a major determinant of synovial expansion and inflammatory maintenance. TNFAIP2 merits attention because inflammation and angiogenesis are two core pathological processes in arthritis. Synovial angiogenesis supports leukocyte recruitment and expansion of the inflamed pannus, while inflammatory mediators drive pain, swelling, and tissue destruction. A factor that sits at the interface of these processes could contribute to both immune amplification and structural progression. Although the functional annotation is brief and uncited in the provided data, TNFAIP2 is still a plausible arthritis-related candidate because it aligns closely with the biology of active synovitis and vascular remodeling.

Finally, the enriched set also includes proteins whose relevance may be more indirect but still conceptually connected to immune recognition in arthritis. B2M is indirectly relevant to arthritis through its central role in major histocompatibility complex class I antigen presentation. Antigen presentation is fundamental to immune recognition and can shape autoreactive as well as antiviral T-cell responses. Although the specific annotation provided focuses on human immunodeficiency virus type 1 epitope presentation rather than arthritis, class I antigen presentation pathways are pertinent to inflammatory arthritides in which adaptive immunity contributes to disease initiation or perpetuation. Therefore, B2M is less directly compelling than proteins linked to leukocyte trafficking, cytokine signaling, or angiogenesis, but it still has conceptual relevance because it participates in the machinery of immune activation.

### immunoglobulin complex (GO:0019814) 

The immunoglobulin complex pathway refers to the biology of antibody-containing protein assemblies formed by two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains, either as membrane-bound antigen receptors on B lymphocytes or as secreted antibodies in tissues, synovial fluid, blood, and lymph. In arthritis, this pathway is important because immunoglobulin complexes do not merely mark immune activation; they can also directly contribute to inflammation, tissue injury, and bone destruction. Secreted immunoglobulins recognize self-antigens, microbial antigens, or modified host proteins and can assemble into soluble or insoluble immune complexes that engage receptors for the constant region of immunoglobulin on monocytes, macrophages, neutrophils, osteoclast precursors, and other effector cells. This receptor engagement promotes production of inflammatory mediators, especially tumor necrosis factor, amplifies complement activation, and enhances recruitment and activation of additional immune cells. In rheumatoid arthritis, classic observations showed that circulating and synovial immune complexes contain immunoglobulin G, immunoglobulin M rheumatoid factor, and sometimes immunoglobulin A, with larger complexes being particularly associated with extra-articular disease. Experimental work further demonstrated that arthritis can be initiated by autoreactive T lymphocytes but then become largely dependent on pathogenic immunoglobulins directed against glucose-6-phosphate isomerase, indicating that antibody complexes may serve as dominant downstream effectors of disease. More recent studies extend this concept by showing that immunoglobulin-containing complexes stimulate monocytes through receptors for the constant region of immunoglobulin and induce tumor necrosis factor production, can activate neutrophils in synovial fluid, and can promote osteoclast formation and local bone erosion. Taken together, this pathway provides a plausible mechanistic link between adaptive autoimmunity, innate inflammatory activation, and structural joint damage.

Consistent with this biological framework, the collected literature indicates that the immunoglobulin complex pathway is strongly implicated in arthritis, especially rheumatoid arthritis, by connecting autoantibody formation with synovial inflammation, cytokine production, and bone damage. A pivotal experimental study showed that in autoimmune arthritis, disease may be initiated by T lymphocyte recognition of the self-antigen glucose-6-phosphate isomerase, but subsequent joint pathology is driven almost entirely by pathogenic immunoglobulins, establishing a direct disease-promoting role for antibody complexes rather than a purely joint-restricted T lymphocyte process [[25]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10576739). In human rheumatoid arthritis, circulating immune complexes composed of immunoglobulin G, immunoglobulin M rheumatoid factor, and immunoglobulin A have been characterized, and larger complexes are associated with extra-articular manifestations, supporting the view that immunoglobulin complex burden and composition may influence disease phenotype [[26]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2029205). Within the joint, soluble and insoluble immunoglobulin aggregates isolated from synovial fluid activate neutrophils through receptors for the constant region of immunoglobulin, especially through cooperative signaling involving receptor classes two and three, thereby promoting oxidant production and inflammatory injury [[27]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7944636). Monocytes from patients with rheumatoid arthritis also show increased expression of receptor for the constant region of immunoglobulin gamma three a, and this increase correlates with tumor necrosis factor production after immune complex stimulation and with poor response to methotrexate, indicating that heightened sensitivity to immunoglobulin complexes may contribute to persistent inflammation and treatment resistance [[28]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22235253). Beyond inflammation, immunoglobulin complexes can influence structural damage: desialylated immunoglobulin G complexes enhance osteoclastogenesis and local bone erosion, suggesting that antibody complexes may directly couple immune activation to bone resorption [[29]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33320370). Broader mechanistic reviews likewise place immune complexes and their receptors near the core of rheumatoid arthritis pathogenesis, upstream of many cytokine cascades [[30]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17121483) [[31]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12969325). Although psoriatic arthritis is often less classically autoantibody-driven than rheumatoid arthritis, studies of synovitis in paradoxical arthritis and precision medicine approaches in psoriatic arthritis still highlight immunoglobulin-related immune phenotypes as clinically informative, suggesting that this pathway may remain relevant across inflammatory arthritides, albeit with disease-specific weight and mechanism [[32]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29657833) [[33]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35372404). Finally, transcriptomic work in knee osteoarthritis identified enrichment of immunoglobulin complex and immunoglobulin-mediated immune response signatures, implying that even degenerative joint disease may contain an immunoglobulin-associated inflammatory component in some contexts [[34]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38012881). Taken together, these findings support the interpretation that the immunoglobulin complex pathway represents a major pathogenic axis in arthritis because it enables autoantibodies and immune complexes to activate innate effector cells, amplify inflammatory mediators, shape clinical heterogeneity, and promote joint erosion.[[25]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10576739) [[26]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2029205) [[27]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7944636) [[28]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22235253) [[29]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33320370) [[30]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17121483) [[31]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12969325) [[32]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29657833) [[33]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35372404) [[34]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38012881) 

Building on this literature-based interpretation, the enrichment result provides a focused protein-level view of the same biological theme. There were 4 arthritis-associated proteins significantly enriched in the immunoglobulin complex pathway, a function centered on antibody-containing assemblies composed of 2 identical heavy chains and 2 identical light chains that operate either as membrane-bound antigen receptors or as secreted antibodies in blood, lymph, tissues, and synovial fluid. In the context of arthritis, this enrichment is biologically notable because immunoglobulin complexes can act not only as markers of immune activation but also as direct drivers of inflammatory pathology, tissue injury, and bone destruction. Quantitatively, the pathway description emphasizes repeated multicomponent interactions involving immunoglobulin-containing complexes, receptors for the constant region of immunoglobulin on monocytes, macrophages, neutrophils, and osteoclast precursors, and downstream induction of inflammatory mediators such as tumor necrosis factor. This places the 4 enriched proteins within a mechanistic framework that connects adaptive autoimmunity to innate effector activation, complement amplification, immune-cell recruitment, and structural joint damage. Clinical and experimental observations further support the relevance of this pathway in arthritis, including the presence of immunoglobulin G, immunoglobulin M rheumatoid factor, and in some cases immunoglobulin A within circulating and synovial immune complexes, as well as evidence that disease initiated by autoreactive T lymphocytes can become strongly dependent on pathogenic immunoglobulins directed against glucose-6-phosphate isomerase. Together, these findings indicate that even a compact set of 4 enriched proteins can map to a highly disease-relevant pathway with potential implications for synovial inflammation, extra-articular manifestations, osteoclast formation, and local bone erosion.

To complement the enrichment result, the interaction network below provides a visual summary of the relationships among these 4 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for interactive inspection.

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Beginning with the most directly connected candidate, CD79B appears particularly relevant to arthritis, especially autoimmune forms such as rheumatoid arthritis. CD79B is a core component of the B cell receptor signaling apparatus, and the cited functional description emphasizes its phosphorylation-dependent role in transmitting antigen-induced signals, including cooperation with kinases involved in nuclear factor kappa B activation and Bruton tyrosine kinase signaling. These pathways are highly pertinent to arthritis because aberrant B cell activation contributes to autoantibody production, antigen presentation, cytokine release, and the maintenance of synovial inflammation. In rheumatoid arthritis and related inflammatory arthritides, dysregulated B cell receptor signaling is mechanistically linked to the survival and activation of autoreactive B cells, which in turn promote chronic joint inflammation and tissue damage. The involvement of CD79B in pre-B cell receptor and B cell receptor signaling, as well as in signaling outcomes such as apoptosis and growth arrest, further suggests that alterations in this axis could influence immune tolerance and the persistence of pathogenic B cell clones. Therefore, CD79B stands out as a biologically meaningful arthritis-related protein because it lies at the center of B cell signaling networks that are already therapeutically implicated in autoimmune joint disease.[[35]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12563261) [[36]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14662906) [[37]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2404338) [[38]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7608542) [[39]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7690139) [[40]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9636152) [[41]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7592958) [[42]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9177269) [[43]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7565679) 

Extending from B cell signaling to innate lymphocyte crosstalk, NCR3LG1 is also of substantial interest in the context of arthritis because it connects innate immune activation with cytokine-driven inflammation. The described function indicates that NCR3LG1 activates natural killer cells and promotes the production of tumor necrosis factor alpha and interferon gamma, two cytokines with well-established roles in inflammatory arthritis. Tumor necrosis factor is a central pathogenic mediator in rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory joint diseases, and interferon gamma can shape synovial immune responses, macrophage activation, and antigen presentation. In addition, the ability of NCR3LG1 and natural cytotoxicity triggering receptor 3 signaling to influence dendritic cell maturation suggests a broader role in coordinating innate and adaptive immunity, potentially enhancing the presentation of arthritogenic antigens and sustaining chronic inflammation in the joint microenvironment. Although the provided entry does not explicitly mention arthritis, this protein remains notable because it is mechanistically linked to natural killer cell activation, dendritic cell crosstalk, and cytokine pathways that are highly relevant to synovitis and immune-mediated joint damage.

In a somewhat different but still potentially related direction, PIGR may have a more indirect but still meaningful connection to arthritis, especially in forms of disease in which mucosal immunity and immunoglobulin A biology are implicated. Its function in the assembly and transport-related handling of polymeric immunoglobulin A and immunoglobulin M suggests relevance to immune exclusion at mucosal surfaces and to the regulation of secretory antibody responses. This is noteworthy because increasing evidence links mucosal immune dysregulation, particularly involving immunoglobulin A responses, with the initiation or amplification of autoimmune arthritis, including rheumatoid arthritis. Immunoglobulin A autoantibodies and mucosal immune activation have been associated with preclinical rheumatoid arthritis and with disease heterogeneity. Thus, although PIGR is not a canonical arthritis gene, its role in polymeric immunoglobulin biology makes it plausibly relevant to mechanisms that connect barrier immunity, antibody maturation, and systemic autoimmunity.

Finally, because no functional annotation was supplied for IGLC2 in the input, its relevance to arthritis cannot be assessed directly from the provided evidence. In general, immunoglobulin constant-region genes can reflect B cell and plasma cell activity, which is often important in autoimmune arthritis; however, without a specific functional description or cited evidence, no robust mechanistic interpretation should be made here.

### Placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[High] (HPA:0381223) 

The pathway labeled “Placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[High]” refers to the abundant formation and maintenance of microvilli on the apical surface of placental syncytiotrophoblasts. Syncytiotrophoblasts form the outer multinucleated epithelial layer of chorionic villi and are directly bathed by maternal blood in the intervillous space. Their microvilli markedly expand the exchange surface for oxygen, nutrients, metabolites, hormones, and signaling molecules, while also contributing to barrier function, mechanosensing, and immunological communication at the maternal fetal interface. In this context, a high microvillus state may be viewed as reflecting structural and functional integrity of the placental exchange membrane. The cited literature further suggests that disruption of this state is associated with pathological stress responses. In acute coronavirus disease 2019, syncytiotrophoblasts show loss of microvilli, vacuolization, apoptosis, and endothelial injury, together with villous stromal swelling and reduced vascular lumen, findings that are consistent with hypoxia, energy deficiency, inflammation, and malperfusion. Similarly, elevated particulate matter exposure is associated with shortened and lost microvilli, endoplasmic reticulum stress, basement membrane thickening, mitochondrial injury, and biochemical evidence of oxidative stress. A broader review of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy further places syncytiotrophoblast and villous dysfunction within a framework of endothelial dysregulation, inflammatory signaling, impaired vascular growth factor balance, and placental hypoxia. Taken together, this pathway may be most appropriately understood as a marker of preserved placental epithelial surface specialization, whereas its reduction may indicate oxidative, inflammatory, and vascular injury.

Against this biological background, the relationship between this pathway and arthritis appears indirect, but it remains biologically plausible through shared mechanisms of chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and immune dysregulation. The pregnancy hypertension review explicitly identifies rheumatoid arthritis as a maternal condition associated with increased risk of hypertensive placental disease, thereby placing arthritis within a clinical context in which abnormal placental villous signaling and syncytiotrophoblast dysfunction may be relevant. In that review, placental disease is linked to endothelial overactivity, inflammatory states, hypoxia, and disturbed vascular signaling involving vascular endothelial growth factor, placental growth factor, soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase, soluble endoglin, transforming growth factor signaling, and reduced corin dependent natriuretic peptide activation. These processes may provide a mechanistic bridge to arthritis because inflammatory arthritis is likewise characterized by systemic endothelial activation, cytokine driven vascular injury, and oxidative stress. The two morphology based studies further support this connection by showing that loss of syncytiotrophoblast microvilli occurs in settings of inflammatory and oxidative injury. Acute coronavirus disease 2019 placentas display microvillus loss together with apoptosis, endothelial dysfunction, placentitis, hypoxia, and malperfusion, while particulate matter exposure causes microvillus shortening and loss accompanied by endoplasmic reticulum stress, mitochondrial damage, and increased oxidative stress markers. Although these studies are not arthritis studies per se, they suggest that the microvillus rich syncytiotrophoblast phenotype is highly sensitive to categories of injury that are also central to arthritis pathobiology. Therefore, in patients with arthritis, especially inflammatory forms, this pathway may be interpreted not as an arthritis specific pathway but rather as a placental structural program that could be secondarily perturbed by the systemic inflammatory and vascular milieu associated with arthritis, potentially contributing to adverse pregnancy related outcomes rather than to joint pathology itself.[[44]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40505896) 

With this conceptual link established, the enrichment results provide a more specific view of how arthritis associated proteins may converge on this placental program. There were 19 arthritis-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway labeled “Placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[High].” This enrichment highlights a protein set linked to preservation of the placental syncytiotrophoblast apical surface, where dense microvillus architecture supports a large exchange interface for oxygen, nutrients, metabolites, hormones, and signaling molecules, while also contributing to barrier integrity, mechanosensing, and immunological communication at the maternal fetal interface. In the biological context summarized for this pathway, a high microvillus state may represent structural and functional integrity, whereas reduction of this state is associated with pathological injury patterns that include microvillus loss, vacuolization, apoptosis, endothelial injury, stromal swelling, reduced vascular lumen, endoplasmic reticulum stress, mitochondrial damage, oxidative stress, inflammation, hypoxia, and malperfusion. Thus, the enrichment of 19 proteins in this pathway suggests that the analyzed arthritis related protein set may converge on processes related to epithelial surface specialization, oxidative and inflammatory stress responses, and vascular dysfunction.

To further contextualize these 19 proteins, the figure below illustrates their protein-protein interaction network, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here for direct network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/61a2d58b-6f6b-4288-9524-22af2c595214.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=4D5563F4CFED12CD)

Building on this network-level view, the functional enrichment analysis identified several significant proteins that may help clarify how this pathway intersects with arthritis related biology. We introduce these proteins in greater detail below.

ACE2 is notable in the context of arthritis because vascular dysfunction, endothelial activation, and thromboinflammatory processes are increasingly recognized as important components of chronic inflammatory joint disease. Its vasodilatory and antithrombotic activities suggest a protective role in limiting microvascular injury and platelet driven inflammation within synovial tissues. In arthritis, particularly rheumatoid arthritis, impaired endothelial homeostasis and reduced nitric oxide bioavailability contribute to synovial hypoxia, leukocyte recruitment, and persistent inflammation. Therefore, ACE2 may be mechanistically relevant through its ability to counterbalance these processes and potentially restrain inflammatory vascular remodeling.

In a related manner, ACTA2 may also be relevant to arthritis because cytoskeletal remodeling underlies several pathogenic processes in the arthritic joint, including fibroblast-like synoviocyte migration, myofibroblast-like contractility, and vascular smooth muscle responses. In inflammatory arthritis, activated stromal cells acquire invasive properties that promote pannus formation and cartilage destruction. Although the provided annotation is general, the role of ACTA2 in motility and contractile architecture makes it a plausible marker of mesenchymal activation, tissue remodeling, and synovial invasion rather than a direct immune mediator.

Along similar lines, BSG stands out less for direct canonical arthritis biology than for its broader implications in cell adhesion and tissue interaction. Adhesion molecules are central to leukocyte trafficking, synovial cell communication, and matrix remodeling in inflamed joints. While the supplied functional description emphasizes neural rather than synovial biology, the adhesive and regulatory properties of BSG suggest potential relevance to inflammatory tissue organization and chronic damage responses. This may be particularly pertinent in arthritis associated pain, neuroimmune crosstalk, or tissue remodeling, although the direct connection appears weaker than for immune or vascular regulators.[[45]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12089450) [[46]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27922006) [[47]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7533044) [[48]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10625334) [[49]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7516497) [[50]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9262180) [[51]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9469574) [[52]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482781) [[53]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482783) [[54]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26335717) [[55]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15953602) [[56]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19158290) [[57]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17640868) 

Moving from adhesion related processes to adaptive immunity, CD74 appears highly relevant to arthritis because antigen presentation through major histocompatibility complex class two pathways is a central mechanism in autoimmune joint inflammation, especially rheumatoid arthritis. By controlling peptide loading onto major histocompatibility complex class two molecules, CD74 directly influences the repertoire of antigens presented to cluster of differentiation four positive T cells. This is important for the initiation and perpetuation of autoreactive immune responses against joint associated or post translationally modified self antigens. Thus, CD74 can be linked to fundamental disease mechanisms involving adaptive immunity, T cell activation, and chronic synovial inflammation.

Consistent with the importance of immune cell trafficking, CD99L2 is particularly interesting for arthritis because leukocyte extravasation into the synovium is a defining event in inflammatory joint disease. The ability of CD99L2 to facilitate passage through the endothelial basement membrane places it at a critical checkpoint in immune cell recruitment. In rheumatoid arthritis and related inflammatory arthritides, sustained infiltration by neutrophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes drives synovitis and tissue destruction. A molecule functioning at this late transmigration step could therefore contribute directly to persistent inflammatory cell accumulation within joints and may represent a biologically meaningful mediator of synovial inflammation.

From the perspective of innate immune sensing, COLEC12 may also be relevant to arthritis because innate immune activation and clearance of modified self components are important in chronic synovial inflammation. Its ability to recognize microbes supports a possible role in triggering or amplifying inflammatory responses, while its capacity to internalize oxidized low density lipoprotein links it to oxidative stress and damage associated molecular patterns, both of which are increasingly implicated in joint pathology. In arthritis, macrophages and endothelial cells encounter oxidatively modified lipids and inflammatory debris within the joint microenvironment; thus, COLEC12 may contribute to inflammatory sensing, phagocytic clearance, and vascular inflammatory interactions.

In contrast to these more direct inflammatory mediators, GFRAL is not a classical arthritis effector, but it may still be relevant to systemic features of inflammatory disease. Chronic arthritis is often accompanied by fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, and altered metabolism, all of which can be influenced by inflammatory mediators. The growth differentiation factor fifteen and glial cell derived neurotrophic factor family receptor alpha like axis is specifically linked to stress induced appetite suppression and metabolic adaptation, suggesting possible relevance to cachexia-like or constitutional manifestations in severe inflammatory arthritis. However, compared with proteins involved directly in immune trafficking, antigen presentation, or vascular inflammation, its connection appears more indirect and likely pertains to systemic disease burden rather than local joint pathology.[[58]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846097) [[59]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846098) [[60]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846099) [[61]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28953886) [[62]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31152154) [[63]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31928886) [[64]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723474) [[65]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593916) [[66]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35202387) [[67]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630958) [[68]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37380764) [[69]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31875646) [[70]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32661391) 

Returning to immune regulation more directly, LAIR1 is one of the strongest arthritis related candidates in this list because it functions as a broad immune checkpoint that dampens both innate and adaptive immune activation. Its inhibitory effects on T cells, B cells, natural killer cells, cytokine production, and dendritic cell differentiation are highly pertinent to autoimmune arthritis, where loss of immune tolerance, excessive cytokine signaling, and pathogenic B cell and T cell responses sustain chronic synovitis. By suppressing interleukin two, interferon gamma, immunoglobulin G, immunoglobulin E, interleukin eight, interleukin ten, and tumor necrosis factor related outputs and limiting nuclear factor kappa B activation, LAIR1 may act as an endogenous brake on inflammatory circuits that otherwise promote joint damage. Reduced LAIR1 signaling or ineffective inhibitory tone could therefore plausibly contribute to persistent synovial inflammation and autoimmunity.

Closely related to this vascular and inflammatory framework, NOS3 also stands out as highly relevant to arthritis because angiogenesis and endothelial activation are central to pannus formation and maintenance of chronic synovitis. The annotation emphasizes vascular endothelial growth factor driven signaling, endothelial migration, permeability, and nitric oxide pathway activation, all of which are hallmarks of inflamed synovial tissue. In rheumatoid arthritis, expanded microvasculature supports leukocyte entry, nutrient delivery to hyperplastic synovium, and perpetuation of inflammatory signaling. Molecules participating in vascular endothelial growth factor dependent endothelial responses therefore have strong mechanistic links to disease progression, especially in relation to synovial neovascularization and vascular permeability.

Extending this discussion to oxidative membrane injury and lipid turnover, PLA2G15 may be relevant to arthritis because lipid remodeling and oxidized phospholipid metabolism are increasingly appreciated as contributors to inflammatory signaling and tissue injury. Its ability to hydrolyze truncated oxidized phospholipids suggests a protective detoxification role during oxidative stress, a condition strongly associated with inflamed arthritic joints. In addition, phospholipid metabolism in macrophages and lysosome related compartments can influence antigen processing, inflammatory mediator generation, and resolution of tissue damage. Therefore, PLA2G15 may be important in controlling lipid derived inflammatory cues and limiting oxidative membrane damage in the synovial environment.[[71]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10092508) [[72]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11790796) [[73]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20410020) [[74]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23958596) [[75]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25727495) [[76]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29724779) [[77]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30830753) [[78]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36823305) 

Finally, TFPI2 is highly pertinent to arthritis because extracellular matrix remodeling is a major determinant of cartilage erosion, synovial invasion, and joint destruction. By inhibiting plasmin mediated proteolysis, TFPI2 could influence activation of matrix degrading cascades and thereby modulate tissue breakdown. Its additional effects on coagulation related proteases are also noteworthy, as coagulation and fibrinolytic pathways intersect with inflammatory signaling in arthritic joints. Consequently, TFPI2 may participate in the balance between destructive matrix turnover and protective restraint of protease activity within the inflamed synovium.

### Skin 2; fibrohistiocytic cells[High] (HPA:0471443) 

The pathway labeled “Skin 2; fibrohistiocytic cells[High]” most plausibly denotes a skin tissue program enriched in fibrohistiocytic stromal cells, a mesenchymal lineage that includes fibroblast-like and histiocyte-like cells involved in extracellular matrix remodeling, inflammatory cue integration, antigen-presenting cell support, and tissue repair. In immunobiological terms, such a pathway is not a single canonical signaling cascade, but rather a cellular state characterized by high abundance or activation of stromal cells that can shape local immunity through cytokine production, matrix turnover, leukocyte recruitment, and cross-talk with dendritic cells and T cells. This concept appears highly relevant to inflammatory arthritis because fibroblast-like stromal cells are central effectors of persistent synovial inflammation, invasive pannus formation, cartilage destruction, and resistance to therapy. Evidence from rheumatoid arthritis indicates that fibroblast-like synovial cells may acquire pathogenic properties, including survival advantages mediated by autophagy and high mobility group box chromosomal protein 1, thereby sustaining inflammation and reducing methotrexate sensitivity. In parallel, skin-directed studies indicate that the skin immune microenvironment contains tightly regulated interactions among innate lymphoid cells, dendritic cells, and adaptive immune populations, suggesting that stromal-rich skin states could contribute to pre-arthritic immune priming, especially in diseases that link skin and joint inflammation such as psoriatic arthritis. Taken together, a fibrohistiocytic cell-high skin pathway may be understood as a barrier-tissue stromal and immune interaction module with potential to influence arthritis initiation, propagation, and therapeutic response.

Building on this biological interpretation, the available literature supports a meaningful, although still cautious, connection between a skin fibrohistiocytic cell-high pathway and arthritis through two complementary mechanisms: first, stromal cell pathogenicity as a direct driver of chronic joint inflammation, and second, skin immune dysregulation as a potential upstream site of arthritis-promoting immune activation. In rheumatoid arthritis, fibroblast-like synovial cells are established disease effectors, and one relevant study demonstrated that these cells resist methotrexate-induced death by activating autophagy through high mobility group box chromosomal protein 1 and Beclin 1, indicating that fibroblast-dominant mesenchymal programs may sustain inflammatory persistence and treatment resistance in arthritis tissues [[79]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26702616). This concept is consistent with broader rheumatoid arthritis biology showing that disease progression can be delayed by early modulation of T cell co-stimulation with abatacept in individuals at risk, implying that tissue-resident stromal and immune networks may already be active before overt synovitis becomes clinically manifest [[80]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38364839). The skin dimension is particularly important for psoriatic arthritis and possibly for preclinical rheumatoid arthritis because skin immune set points are shaped by local cellular interactions; notably, a recent study showed that skin type 2 innate lymphoid cells regulate dendritic cell homeostasis and activation, thereby influencing downstream adaptive immunity in a sex-dependent manner, which provides a mechanistic framework whereby a stromal-rich skin niche could facilitate inflammatory immune priming relevant to arthritis susceptibility [[81]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38574174). Additional studies in psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis further support a skin-to-joint axis by showing that altered memory T helper cell states accompany early and subclinical psoriatic arthritis, even before a fully established arthritic phenotype is present [[82]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35045868), and that early biological treatment targeting interleukin 17 improves both skin and axial articular manifestations, consistent with shared pathogenic circuits across barrier tissue and musculoskeletal compartments. Collectively, these findings suggest that a “Skin 2; fibrohistiocytic cells[High]” pathway may mark a pro-inflammatory stromal microenvironment in the skin that either mirrors or contributes to the fibroblast-centered, immune-amplifying processes that characterize arthritis, especially in rheumatoid arthritis through fibroblast pathogenicity and in psoriatic arthritis through coordinated skin and joint immune activation.[[79]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26702616) [[80]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38364839) [[81]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38574174) [[82]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35045868) 

With this conceptual background in place, the enrichment results provide a quantitative layer of support for the potential relevance of this pathway to arthritis biology. There were 25 arthritis-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway labeled “Skin 2; fibrohistiocytic cells[High],” a stromal and immune-interaction program that appears highly relevant to arthritis because fibrohistiocytic mesenchymal cells contribute to extracellular matrix remodeling, inflammatory signal integration, leukocyte recruitment, tissue repair, and persistence of pathogenic fibroblast-like states within inflamed joint and barrier tissues. In the context of arthritis, the enrichment of 25 proteins in this pathway supports a quantitatively substantial involvement of stromal-cell-centered biology, consistent with the concept that fibroblast-like pathogenic programs may amplify chronic inflammation, promote invasive tissue behavior, and shape cross-talk with dendritic cells and T cells, thereby influencing disease initiation, propagation, and treatment response. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 25 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is also provided for direct network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/5448f650-7fd7-4667-afa3-ee0f5fa39db6.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=4FC372F3B58265F4)

To further clarify how this enriched set may relate to arthritis, the function enrichment analysis highlighted several proteins with plausible immunological, stromal, and vascular relevance. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

CD14 is one of the most arthritis-relevant proteins in this list because it sits at the interface between innate immune sensing and inflammatory cytokine production, two central features of inflammatory joint disease. Its ability to initiate lipopolysaccharide- and lipopeptide-driven signaling through toll-like receptor pathways directly connects it to nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation and downstream release of proinflammatory mediators, which are major drivers of synovitis, macrophage activation, and tissue destruction in rheumatoid arthritis and related arthritides. The relevance of CD14 is particularly strong in the context of arthritis because synovial macrophages and monocytes are abundant in inflamed joints, and exaggerated innate immune activation is known to amplify tumor necrosis factor, interleukin 1, and interleukin 6 signaling networks. Moreover, CD14-dependent recognition of microbial products is mechanistically pertinent to forms of arthritis in which infection or dysregulated host-microbe interactions may contribute to disease initiation or exacerbation. Thus, among the listed proteins, CD14 stands out as a plausible upstream regulator of joint inflammation and a marker of pathogenic innate immune activation.[[83]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16148141) [[84]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15895089) [[85]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8612135) [[86]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19362712) 

In a closely related manner, the next protein further emphasizes the importance of macrophage-centered biology within chronically inflamed tissues. CD163 is highly relevant to arthritis because macrophage activation is a defining feature of chronically inflamed synovium. The note that soluble CD163 may be anti-inflammatory and can monitor macrophage activation is especially important in arthritis research, where macrophage-derived pathways strongly correlate with disease activity, synovial inflammation, and therapeutic response. In rheumatoid arthritis, activated synovial macrophages contribute to pannus formation, cytokine production, and joint damage; therefore, a macrophage-associated marker such as CD163 has both mechanistic and biomarker significance. Its anti-inflammatory implication also raises the possibility that CD163 reflects compensatory pathways attempting to restrain tissue injury. For these reasons, CD163 stands out as a clinically meaningful molecule for understanding inflammatory burden and potentially stratifying arthritis severity.

Beyond macrophage activation alone, complement-associated mechanisms may provide an additional layer through which innate immunity contributes to joint pathology. Although the provided annotation emphasizes microbial interaction with Epstein-Barr virus, C1QA remains noteworthy in arthritis because complement activation is deeply implicated in synovial inflammation and immune complex-mediated tissue injury. Complement components contribute to leukocyte recruitment, vascular permeability, and amplification of inflammatory cascades within arthritic joints. C1q-related biology is also relevant to clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic debris, processes that are often dysregulated in autoimmune arthritis. The specific mention of Epstein-Barr virus is additionally interesting because viral triggers have long been investigated as possible contributors to autoimmunity, including rheumatoid arthritis. Therefore, C1QA may be relevant not only through complement-mediated inflammation but also through potential links between infection, aberrant immune activation, and chronic joint disease.

Shifting from soluble inflammatory systems to cell trafficking, adhesion-related proteins may help explain how inflammatory cells accumulate and persist within diseased joints. ICAM3 is relevant to arthritis because leukocyte adhesion, retention, and clearance are central determinants of synovial inflammation. Through its interaction with beta-2 integrins, ICAM3 may influence immune-cell communication and trafficking within inflamed tissues. Particularly important is its role in the phagocytosis of apoptotic neutrophils by macrophages, since defective clearance of dying inflammatory cells can prolong synovitis and promote secondary necrosis, thereby intensifying tissue damage. Neutrophils are abundant in inflammatory joint effusions, especially in active rheumatoid arthritis and crystal-associated arthritis, making molecules involved in their resolution biologically meaningful. Thus, ICAM3 may contribute both to leukocyte recruitment and to the resolution phase of inflammation, two processes that are often imbalanced in arthritis.[[87]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1448173) [[88]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23775590) 

Consistent with this trafficking theme, transendothelial migration represents another necessary step for sustaining inflammatory infiltrates in synovial tissue. CD99L2 is of particular interest in arthritis because leukocyte extravasation into synovial tissue is a prerequisite for persistent joint inflammation. Its role in enabling immune cells to cross the endothelial basement membrane places it directly within the cellular trafficking machinery that supports synovitis. In inflammatory arthritis, the accumulation of monocytes, macrophages, and other leukocytes in the joint is a major pathogenic event that sustains cytokine production and tissue destruction. Proteins that regulate this late step of transmigration are therefore mechanistically significant, as they may determine the intensity and persistence of inflammatory infiltrates. CD99L2 consequently stands out as a plausible contributor to immune-cell entry into arthritic joints and a potential modulator of inflammatory burden.

Alongside immune-cell influx, vascular remodeling is another major feature of chronically inflamed synovium, making angiogenesis-related proteins especially informative. COL18A1 is highly relevant to arthritis because pathological angiogenesis is a hallmark of chronically inflamed synovium. Expansion of the synovial microvasculature supplies nutrients, facilitates leukocyte entry, and supports pannus formation, thereby promoting disease persistence and joint destruction. The anti-angiogenic properties of COL18A1, including inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor A-kinase insert domain receptor signaling and endothelial migration, suggest that it may function as an endogenous brake on these processes. This is particularly important in rheumatoid arthritis, where vascular endothelial growth factor-driven neovascularization is strongly linked to active synovitis. Therefore, COL18A1 stands out as a protein with a potentially protective role, and its biology may be informative for understanding how angiogenic balance influences arthritis progression.[[89]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [[90]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123) 

In contrast, other enriched proteins may point toward pathways that promote rather than restrain stromal expansion and vascular growth. FGFBP1 is notable in the context of arthritis because it integrates growth factor signaling, cell proliferation, and angiogenesis, all of which are central to synovial hyperplasia and pannus development. Its ability to support fibroblast growth factor and integrin-mediated signaling, together with its potent mitogenic and pro-angiogenic effects, suggests that it could enhance fibroblast-like synoviocyte expansion and vascular remodeling in inflamed joints. These processes are especially relevant to rheumatoid arthritis, where excessive synovial proliferation and neovascularization sustain chronic inflammation and facilitate invasive tissue behavior. In contrast to anti-angiogenic regulators such as COL18A1, FGFBP1 may represent a pathway that promotes the pathogenic stromal response in arthritis. Its functional profile therefore makes it one of the more compelling candidates for involvement in joint remodeling and persistent inflammation.[[91]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8663044) [[92]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28302677) [[93]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1721615) [[94]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3732516) [[95]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3964259) [[96]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23469107) [[97]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29501879) 

Related to this vascular context, stress-response proteins may also shape how stromal and endothelial compartments adapt to persistent inflammation. HSPB6 may have a meaningful, although more indirect, connection to arthritis through its roles in cellular stress responses, vascular regulation, and angiogenesis. Arthritis is characterized by chronic inflammatory stress within the joint microenvironment, and chaperone proteins can influence how stromal and vascular cells respond to inflammatory injury. The reported association with kinase insert domain receptor-related angiogenesis is of particular interest because vascular remodeling contributes to synovial expansion and leukocyte recruitment. In addition, stress-protective proteins may affect the survival of resident joint cells exposed to cytokine-rich conditions. While HSPB6 is not as directly implicated in immune activation as CD14 or CD163, its functions suggest potential relevance to the vascular and stress-adaptation components of arthritis pathobiology.

From vascular adaptation, the discussion naturally extends to cytoskeletal organization, which underlies the invasive behavior of pathogenic stromal cells. ACTA2 is relevant to arthritis because cytoskeletal remodeling and cell motility are essential for the behavior of myofibroblast-like and smooth muscle-like cells in inflamed synovium and vasculature. In chronic arthritis, activated fibroblast-like synoviocytes acquire invasive properties that depend on actin dynamics, enabling migration, matrix remodeling, and cartilage invasion. ACTA2 is also often associated with contractile stromal phenotypes, which may contribute to tissue remodeling and fibrosis-like changes in long-standing disease. Although ACTA2 is a general structural protein rather than a specific inflammatory mediator, its role in motility makes it biologically relevant to the aggressive stromal phenotype that characterizes destructive arthritis.

A similar logic applies to additional regulators of actin dynamics and adhesion, which may further influence synovial lining expansion and tissue invasion. ENAH may be relevant to arthritis because actin remodeling, adhesion, and proliferative control are central to the pathogenic behavior of synovial fibroblasts. In inflammatory arthritis, fibroblast-like synoviocytes display enhanced spreading, migration, and invasive interactions with cartilage and extracellular matrix. A protein such as ENAH, which regulates cytoskeletal organization and adhesion, could therefore influence the structural and migratory properties of these cells. Its reported role in proliferation control is also notable, given that synovial lining hyperplasia is a key pathological feature of rheumatoid arthritis. Although the evidence provided does not directly mention joint disease, ENAH stands out as a plausible modulator of stromal-cell behavior relevant to arthritis progression.

In addition to structural regulators, receptor-mediated signaling pathways may modulate how inflammatory and stromal cells respond to the joint microenvironment. KIT is potentially relevant to arthritis because receptor tyrosine kinase signaling affects mast cells, progenitor cells, and stromal responses, all of which can contribute to joint inflammation. The specific annotation emphasizes negative regulation of KIT through ubiquitination, which is important because dysregulated receptor signaling can amplify inflammatory or tissue-remodeling responses. In arthritis, mast cells and stromal cells have been implicated in cytokine production, vascular changes, and local immune activation; thus, mechanisms controlling KIT abundance may influence disease intensity. While this entry is less direct than those for innate immune receptors or adhesion molecules, KIT remains of interest as part of the broader signaling networks that modulate inflammatory cell function in the joint.

Finally, cell-cycle regulation provides another perspective on how persistent synovial expansion may develop over time in inflammatory disease. MAD1L1 has a more indirect but still potentially meaningful connection to arthritis through its role in cell-cycle control. Synovial hyperplasia in inflammatory arthritis reflects, in part, aberrant proliferation and persistence of stromal and immune cells. Proteins governing mitotic fidelity may therefore influence the expansion, survival, or stress responses of these cell populations. Although MAD1L1 is not a canonical inflammatory mediator, pathways controlling cell division can shape the aggressive phenotype of synovial tissue, especially in rheumatoid arthritis where fibroblast-like synoviocytes exhibit tumor-like proliferative features. Thus, MAD1L1 may be of interest as a marker of proliferative activity rather than a primary driver of inflammation.[[98]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15024386) [[99]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29162720) [[100]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10700282) [[101]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11804586)

### specific granule (GO:0042581) 

The specific granule is a secretory organelle that is characteristic of mature neutrophils and contains a membranous, tubular internal architecture. It stores a defined set of antimicrobial and inflammatory proteins, including lactoferrin, lysozyme, vitamin B12 binding protein, and elastase, many of which are released into the extracellular space during neutrophil activation. In biologic terms, this pathway represents the formation, storage, mobilization, and exocytosis of neutrophil specific granule contents, together with their downstream effects on host defense and tissue inflammation. Because neutrophils are among the earliest and most abundant leukocytes recruited to inflamed joints, the specific granule pathway is highly relevant to inflammatory arthritis. Its cargo proteins can amplify inflammation, remodel extracellular matrix, influence cytokine networks, and contribute to the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps. Lactoferrin is particularly important as a canonical constituent of neutrophil specific granules and has been used as a highly selective marker of neutrophils in inflammatory settings, including experimental arthritis. Thus, the specific granule pathway is best understood as a core neutrophil effector program that links granulocyte maturation to degranulation, extracellular antimicrobial defense, and collateral tissue injury in chronic joint disease.

Against this biologic background, the cited studies collectively suggest that the specific granule pathway may be linked to arthritis primarily through neutrophil activation, degranulation, and release of granule-derived inflammatory mediators within the joint microenvironment. A key piece of evidence is that lactoferrin, one of the defining proteins of neutrophil specific granules, serves as a highly specific neutrophil marker and can localize inflammatory foci in a mouse arthritis model, indicating that specific granule biology is active at sites of articular inflammation and may be exploited to monitor disease-associated neutrophil accumulation [[102]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29478905). Additional support comes from rheumatoid arthritis transcriptomic work showing that circulating neutrophils display marked phenotypic plasticity and that expression of neutrophil granule protein genes predicts therapeutic response to tumor necrosis factor inhibition, implying that granule-related neutrophil states are mechanistically tied to disease heterogeneity and inflammatory signaling in rheumatoid arthritis [[103]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27733572). The relevance of granule pathways is further strengthened by the observation that dipeptidyl peptidase one, a granule-associated protease activator in immune cells, correlates with arthritis severity in collagen-induced arthritis rats, suggesting that granule protease activation tracks with disease progression [[104]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27771442). Although one cited study focuses on antifungal immunity rather than arthritis, it demonstrates that Bruton's tyrosine kinase is required for neutrophil activation, oxidative burst, and granule release, reinforcing the broader principle that signaling pathways controlling neutrophil degranulation can strongly shape inflammatory tissue responses and may therefore represent plausible regulators of arthritic pathology [[105]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38696257). The importance of granule-derived products also intersects with neutrophil extracellular trap biology, because extracellular traps are composed in part of granule proteins and have been implicated in gouty arthritis as both inflammatory amplifiers and regulators of crystal containment, highlighting how granule cargo can participate directly in joint inflammation and tissue damage [[106]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41254711). Finally, several arthritis studies in the list converge on tumor necrosis factor, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells, toll-like receptor four, and nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-like receptor pyrin domain containing three inflammasome signaling as central inflammatory axes in rheumatoid arthritis, and these pathways are well known drivers and consequences of neutrophil activation and degranulation, providing a disease context in which specific granule release is likely to contribute to synovitis, cartilage injury, and sustained innate immune activation [[107]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41866004) [[108]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41389887) [[109]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39608616). Taken together, the available evidence suggests that the specific granule pathway may be more than a marker of neutrophil presence in arthritis and could represent a functional effector system influencing inflammatory burden, protease activity, extracellular trap formation, and treatment responsiveness across inflammatory joint diseases.[[102]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29478905) [[103]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27733572) [[104]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27771442) [[105]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38696257) [[106]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41254711) [[107]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41866004) [[108]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41389887) [[109]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39608616) 

Consistent with this literature-based interpretation, the enrichment analysis also points to a quantitatively substantial neutrophil-centered signal.
