Consistent with this emphasis on tissue remodeling, the next entry appears to describe a vascular endothelial growth factor receptor pathway that may also be highly relevant to arthritis. Despite the apparent naming inconsistency in the provided annotation, the listed function clearly describes a vascular endothelial growth factor receptor pathway. Pathologic angiogenesis and increased vascular permeability are defining features of inflamed synovium, enabling persistent leukocyte influx and expansion of pannus tissue. The described signaling outputs, including endothelial migration, survival, actin remodeling, and induction of nitric oxide production, are all processes implicated in synovial hypervascularity and inflammatory edema. Vascular endothelial growth factor-driven signaling is well established as a contributor to rheumatoid arthritis progression, and proteins mediating these effects can influence both inflammation and structural joint damage. Accordingly, this entry stands out because vascular remodeling is a major component of arthritis pathogenesis.

This focus on structural damage leads naturally to OSCAR, which is one of the most directly arthritis-relevant proteins in the list because osteoclast differentiation is a central mechanism of bone erosion in inflammatory arthritis, especially rheumatoid arthritis. Bone destruction in arthritis is not merely a byproduct of inflammation; it is actively driven by osteoclastogenic pathways at the synovial-bone interface. A receptor that specifically regulates osteoclastogenesis therefore has immediate mechanistic relevance to structural damage, radiographic progression, and irreversible disability. OSCAR stands out because it links immune activation to skeletal pathology, making it particularly important for understanding erosive disease phenotypes.

Another protein that may connect inflammatory signaling with joint damage is PLA2G2A, which is highly pertinent to arthritis because it can directly fuel inflammatory lipid mediator production and influence cell-matrix signaling. By releasing arachidonic acid from phospholipids, PLA2G2A provides substrate for downstream synthesis of prostaglandins and leukotrienes, both of which are major mediators of pain, swelling, leukocyte recruitment, and tissue injury in arthritic joints. Its additional integrin-activating function suggests that it may also modulate synovial cell adhesion, migration, and proliferation, potentially contributing to pannus formation. The combination of enzymatic pro-inflammatory activity and non-catalytic signaling effects makes PLA2G2A a particularly compelling candidate in arthritis biology.[[194]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10358193) [[195]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11694541) [[196]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8425615) [[197]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27292189) 

In a similar vein, PLAUR is relevant to arthritis because the urokinase plasminogen activator receptor system is closely linked to extracellular matrix remodeling, cell migration, and invasive behavior of synovial cells. In inflammatory arthritis, excessive pericellular proteolysis contributes to cartilage degradation, basement membrane disruption, and leukocyte trafficking into the joint. Beyond proteolysis, the signaling functions of PLAUR may support motility and activation of fibroblast-like synoviocytes and immune cells, thereby promoting chronic synovitis and tissue invasion. This makes PLAUR an important candidate for connecting inflammatory activation with structural joint damage.[[115]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15677461) 

Beyond matrix remodeling, humoral effector systems may also contribute to joint injury, and C9 stands out because complement activation is an established contributor to inflammatory arthritis. Formation of the membrane attack complex can promote direct tissue injury, amplify synovial inflammation, and enhance recruitment and activation of leukocytes. In arthritic joints, complement components can be activated by immune complexes and damaged tissue, thereby sustaining inflammatory cascades. As the pore-forming component of the terminal complement pathway, C9 is especially relevant to the effector phase of complement-mediated damage within synovium and cartilage.[[198]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26841934) [[199]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9212048) [[200]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9634479) [[201]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30111885) [[202]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/4055801) 

Balancing this pro-inflammatory complement activity, C4BPB is noteworthy in arthritis because it represents a counter-regulatory component of the complement system. Since excessive classical pathway activation can contribute to immune complex-driven synovitis and tissue damage, proteins that restrain complement activation may influence disease severity and the extent of bystander injury. The function of C4BPB suggests a protective role by limiting propagation of complement cascades in inflamed tissue. In arthritis, such regulators are important because disease outcome often depends not only on inflammatory triggers but also on the adequacy of endogenous mechanisms that contain tissue-damaging effector responses.

Resolution of inflammation is also shaped by cellular interactions, and ICAM3 is relevant to arthritis because leukocyte adhesion and clearance of apoptotic cells are both key determinants of whether inflammation resolves or persists. The ability of ICAM3 to mediate interactions with beta-2 integrins suggests a role in immune cell trafficking and cell-cell communication in synovial tissue. Particularly important is its contribution to macrophage phagocytosis of apoptotic neutrophils, a process central to resolution of inflammation. Defects in apoptotic cell clearance can prolong synovitis and promote secondary necrosis, thereby increasing inflammatory mediator release. ICAM3 therefore stands out as a molecule potentially linked to both inflammatory cell retention and defective resolution in arthritis.[[87]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1448173) [[88]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23775590) 

A related connection between myeloid activation and skeletal damage is suggested by the next entry. Although the provided functional description appears to correspond to the triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells two-associated adaptor pathway rather than triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells two alone, the biology described is highly relevant to arthritis. Two aspects are especially important: first, the promotion of myeloid and neutrophil activation, which can intensify synovial inflammation; second, the requirement for osteoclast cytoskeletal organization and multinucleation, which directly links this pathway to bone erosion. In inflammatory arthritis, osteoclast formation at the pannus-bone interface is a major cause of irreversible structural damage. Thus, this entry stands out because it integrates immune activation with osteoclastogenesis, two core processes in arthritis pathogenesis.[[203]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15471863) [[204]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647200) [[205]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728241) [[206]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16715077) [[207]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21727189) [[208]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18957693) [[209]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18685038) [[210]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690660) [[211]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21257958) [[212]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18691974) [[213]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12569157) [[214]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14969392) [[189]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17086186) 

This interplay between inflammatory signaling and tissue persistence is also reflected in TNFRSF1B, which is highly relevant to arthritis because tumor necrosis factor signaling is one of the central pathogenic pathways in rheumatoid arthritis and related inflammatory arthritides. The annotation emphasizes nuclear factor kappa B and c-Jun N-terminal kinase activation, both of which drive expression of inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, adhesion molecules, and matrix-degrading enzymes in synovial tissue. Its role in balancing survival and apoptosis is also important, since resistance of synovial fibroblasts and inflammatory cells to apoptosis contributes to chronic synovial hyperplasia. TNFRSF1B therefore stands out as a plausible mediator of sustained tumor necrosis factor-dependent inflammation and tissue persistence in arthritic joints.

Moving to a more indirect candidate, ADA2 is less directly established than classical immune mediators, but it may still be relevant to arthritis through neuroimmune regulation. Adrenergic signaling can shape leukocyte activation, vascular tone, and pain-related inflammatory responses. Because synovial inflammation is influenced by autonomic and catecholaminergic inputs, receptors that suppress adenylate cyclase signaling may alter inflammatory cell behavior or local vascular responses. This makes ADA2 an interesting, though more indirect, candidate in the broader pathophysiology of arthritis.

At the level of cellular mechanics, BAIAP2 is potentially relevant to arthritis because cytoskeletal remodeling is essential for migration and invasive behavior of immune cells and fibroblast-like synoviocytes. In rheumatoid arthritis, pathogenic synoviocytes acquire enhanced motility and tissue-invasive properties that depend on actin reorganization. A protein that supports cell division control protein forty-two homolog- and ras-related C3 botulinum toxin substrate one-dependent membrane dynamics may therefore contribute to leukocyte trafficking, pannus invasion, and possibly cartilage destruction. Although not a canonical arthritis gene, BAIAP2 stands out as a plausible regulator of the cellular mechanics underlying joint inflammation and tissue invasion.

Finally, BRK1 is of interest in arthritis because actin-remodeling machinery influences immune cell migration, phagocytosis, and the invasive phenotype of synovial fibroblasts. Through its role in the WASP family verprolin-homologous protein-Arp2/3 pathway, BRK1 may affect lamellipodia formation and cell motility, processes highly relevant to leukocyte recruitment into joints and pannus expansion across cartilage surfaces. While the cited annotation is not arthritis-specific, the underlying cytoskeletal function is mechanistically compatible with disease processes that depend on aberrant cell movement and tissue invasion.[[215]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27605705)

### Matrix metalloproteinases (WP:WP129) 

Matrix metalloproteinases are a family of zinc-dependent endopeptidases that mediate controlled degradation and remodeling of extracellular matrix components, including collagens, proteoglycans, gelatin, and other structural molecules of cartilage, synovium, tendon, and bone. They are synthesized as inactive precursor proteins and require post-translational activation, after which their activity is tightly restrained by tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases. In healthy joints, this proteolytic system contributes to physiological matrix turnover, tissue repair, and remodeling. In inflammatory and degenerative joint disease, however, the balance between matrix metalloproteinases and their inhibitors becomes disturbed, leading to excessive extracellular matrix destruction and altered cellular signaling. Beyond direct matrix cleavage, matrix metalloproteinases can regulate cytokines, chemokines, receptors, angiogenesis, oxidative stress responses, and immune cell behavior, thereby linking structural damage to inflammation and immunity. Distinct family members have partially specialized roles in arthritis: interstitial collagenases and stromelysins participate in cartilage collagen and proteoglycan degradation, gelatinases contribute to matrix remodeling and inflammatory cell migration, and collagenase thirteen is especially important in osteoarthritis because of its potent cleavage of type two collagen. Overall, current evidence places matrix metalloproteinases at the intersection of synovial inflammation, fibroblast pathogenic activation, cartilage erosion, bone destruction, and biomarker development, while also indicating that their net effect depends on disease context, timing, tissue localization, and the counterbalancing action of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases.

Building on this biological framework, the collected literature suggests that the matrix metalloproteinase pathway is a central driver of arthritis pathogenesis across rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, septic arthritis, spondyloarthritis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis because it couples inflammatory activation to irreversible joint tissue destruction. Broad reviews indicate that matrix metalloproteinases are consistently elevated in arthritic joints and, together with other proteases, degrade proteoglycans, collagens, and additional extracellular matrix constituents, thereby promoting cartilage loss and structural remodeling; in rheumatoid arthritis this proteolysis can also generate remnant epitopes that perpetuate autoimmunity, whereas in osteoarthritis collagenase thirteen produced by chondrocytes is a key effector of mechanically and inflammatory induced cartilage degeneration [[216]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37161083) [[217]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37522140) [[218]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36647647). Mechanistically, synovial fibroblasts emerge as a major cellular source of pathogenic matrix metalloproteinases: disease-associated fibroblasts are polarized toward tissue-destructive states by transcriptional regulators such as ETS proto-oncogene one, which coordinates matrix metalloproteinase expression together with receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa B ligand, thereby promoting cartilage and bone damage even when inflammation is not proportionally changed [[219]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35999392). Multiple upstream inflammatory circuits induce this pathway in arthritis, including interleukin one beta, tumor necrosis factor, interleukin seventeen A, granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor, mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, nuclear factor kappa B signaling, Janus kinase two and signal transducer and activator of transcription three signaling, oxidative stress, and microRNA-mediated suppression of suppressor of cytokine signaling three; these signals converge on enhanced expression of matrix metalloproteinases such as matrix metalloproteinase one, matrix metalloproteinase three, matrix metalloproteinase nine, and matrix metalloproteinase thirteen in synovial fibroblasts and joint tissues, amplifying inflammation, pannus invasiveness, osteoclastogenesis, and matrix destruction [[220]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32071294) [[221]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29394098) [[222]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26081345) [[223]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36427113) [[224]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17129374). Experimental arthritis studies further show that matrix metalloproteinase dysregulation is temporally linked to acute inflammatory phases and proteoglycan loss, while the balance with tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinoproteinases, especially tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases three, influences the extent of damage [[225]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15642138) [[216]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37161083). Clinically, circulating or local levels of matrix metalloproteinases, particularly matrix metalloproteinase three and matrix metalloproteinase nine, correlate with disease activity, structural progression, and treatment response in rheumatoid arthritis and spondyloarthritis, and effective therapies such as rituximab or experimental interventions including nuclear receptor subfamily one group D member one agonism, kefir peptides, melatonin, curcumin-related strategies, and other matrix metalloproteinase-targeted approaches reduce matrix metalloproteinase expression in parallel with improvement in synovitis, cartilage preservation, and reduced bone erosion [[226]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25190551) [[227]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35049445) [[228]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28420081) [[220]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32071294) [[229]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36682523) [[230]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38423225). Taken together, these publications support the view that the matrix metalloproteinase pathway is not merely a downstream marker of arthritis but rather a multifunctional pathogenic network that integrates inflammatory signaling, fibroblast and macrophage activation, extracellular matrix degradation, and bone remodeling, making it highly relevant for biomarker development, patient stratification, and targeted therapy.[[216]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37161083) [[220]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32071294) [[217]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37522140) [[224]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17129374) [[225]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15642138) [[231]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38035026) [[219]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35999392) [[227]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35049445) [[228]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28420081) [[226]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25190551) [[229]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36682523) [[218]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36647647) [[221]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29394098) [[223]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36427113) [[222]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26081345) [[230]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38423225) 

To connect this literature-based interpretation with the pathway-level enrichment result, the identified protein set may be viewed as a compact representation of the broader biological processes described above. There were 6 arthritis-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing matrix metalloproteinases as zinc-dependent endopeptidases that regulate extracellular matrix degradation, matrix remodeling, inflammatory signaling, immune cell behavior, angiogenesis, oxidative stress responses, cartilage erosion, and bone destruction. In quantitative terms, this enrichment set contains 6 proteins linked to a single highly disease-relevant biological process in arthritis, supporting a focused functional signal centered on dysregulated extracellular matrix turnover, synovial inflammation, and joint tissue damage, with particular relevance to cartilage, synovium, tendon, and bone biology. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 6 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage can be accessed through the embedded link for direct network inspection and evidence review.

### cargo receptor activity (GO:0038024) 

Cargo receptor activity is a membrane trafficking function in which transmembrane proteins recognize selected extracellular or intracellular materials and couple them to vesicle formation machinery, thereby supporting efficient and specific delivery of cargo into transport vesicles. In general cell biology, this process is essential for endocytosis, secretory trafficking, lysosomal delivery, extracellular protein clearance, and selective autophagy. Cargo receptors act by simultaneously binding cargo molecules and vesicle coat adaptors, allowing cells to internalize soluble particles, present signaling ligands, remove damaged proteins, and direct protein complexes toward degradation or recycling pathways. In the context of immunity and tissue homeostasis, cargo receptor activity may be particularly important because it governs the uptake of inflammatory particles, extracellular vesicles, immune complexes, and misfolded proteins, all of which can shape cytokine production, antigen handling, and cellular stress responses. The publications provided suggest that this pathway is relevant to arthritis through several related mechanisms, including receptor-dependent uptake of calciprotein particles by monocytes, receptor-mediated delivery of chaperone-bound damaged proteins to macrophages, extracellular vesicle communication with immune cells, and selective autophagic cargo recognition in joint tissues. Taken together, these observations place cargo receptor activity at the interface of inflammation, proteostasis, vesicle trafficking, and tissue degeneration in both rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis.  

Building on this general biological framework, the collected literature further supports a potentially meaningful connection between cargo receptor activity and arthritis by showing that receptor-guided vesicular uptake and cargo delivery may either amplify or restrain joint inflammation. The strongest direct evidence comes from rheumatoid arthritis, where increased extracellular calcium in inflamed joints activates the calcium-sensing receptor on monocytes and drives macropinocytic uptake of calciprotein particles; this enhanced particle internalization increases lysosomal activity, activates the NLR family pyrin domain containing 3 inflammasome, and promotes interleukin 1 beta release, with rheumatoid arthritis monocytes showing heightened receptor expression, greater particle uptake, and stronger inflammatory responses than controls, indicating that cargo internalization is functionally linked to disease-associated innate immune activation [[232]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32843625). A related extracellular cargo-handling mechanism is described for human alpha two macroglobulin, which after oxidative modification acquires enhanced chaperone activity and delivers misfolded protein cargo to lipoprotein receptors on macrophages; because oxidative protein damage is implicated in arthritis, this receptor-mediated clearance pathway is relevant to how inflamed tissues may either resolve or perpetuate proteotoxic inflammation [[233]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24799681). Additional studies extend the concept from inflammatory particle uptake to extracellular vesicle cargo transfer: apoptotic vesicles can directly engage cluster of differentiation four positive T cells through exposed phosphatidylserine and suppress proximal T cell receptor signaling, thereby reducing T helper type seventeen differentiation, inflammation, and joint erosion in murine arthritis, suggesting that vesicle-associated cargo recognition can also be anti-inflammatory and tissue protective [[234]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37056273). Likewise, serum exosomes in rheumatoid arthritis carry proteins such as amyloid A and lymphatic vessel endothelial hyaluronic acid receptor one that correlate with disease activity, supporting the idea that vesicle cargo composition and trafficking are integrated with arthritis pathobiology and may reflect active intercellular communication networks in disease [[235]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28569211). In osteoarthritis, a more direct mechanistic link to cargo receptor biology is provided by the finding that coiled-coil domain containing fifty functions as a selective autophagy cargo receptor whose palmitoylation promotes autophagic degradation of mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase four, suppresses mitogen-activated protein kinase and c-Jun N-terminal kinase signaling, reduces chondrocyte senescence, and alleviates disease progression, suggesting that cargo receptor-dependent intracellular degradation may help protect joint tissues from degenerative damage [[236]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41566717). Taken together, these studies indicate that cargo receptor activity is relevant to arthritis because it controls the selective uptake, transfer, and degradation of inflammatory particles, damaged proteins, extracellular vesicle contents, and signaling regulators, thereby influencing inflammasome activation, adaptive immune modulation, cellular stress handling, and cartilage preservation.[[232]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32843625) [[233]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24799681) [[234]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37056273) [[235]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28569211) [[236]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41566717) 

With this literature context in place, the enrichment results provide an additional layer of support for the relevance of this pathway in arthritis. There were 11 arthritis-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of cargo receptor activity, a membrane trafficking function that mediates selective cargo recognition and coupling to vesicle formation machinery. This functional category is biologically relevant to arthritis because it connects inflammatory particle uptake, extracellular vesicle handling, damaged protein clearance, lysosomal targeting, and selective autophagic cargo recognition, all of which are central to synovial inflammation, macrophage activation, proteostasis imbalance, and joint tissue degeneration in both rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis. The enrichment of 11 proteins in this pathway indicates a concentrated signal linking vesicle-directed cargo selection to arthritis-associated cellular dysfunction, particularly through receptor-dependent uptake of calciprotein particles by monocytes, receptor-mediated transfer of chaperone-bound damaged proteins to macrophages, and extracellular vesicle communication that can amplify cytokine production and tissue stress responses. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 11 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here for direct network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/6e8c0ce7-3a96-4516-855c-53125154157a.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=952481229011AE0E)

To further clarify how this enrichment signal may relate to disease biology, the following paragraphs introduce several of the significant proteins identified in the analysis. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
Among the listed proteins, CXCL16 stands out as the most directly relevant to arthritis because it integrates lipid scavenging with leukocyte recruitment, two processes that are highly pertinent to chronic synovial inflammation. Its ability to induce chemotaxis and calcium mobilization indicates an active role in immune-cell trafficking and activation, which are central features of inflammatory arthritis, particularly rheumatoid arthritis, where recruitment of T cells, monocytes, and macrophages into the synovium drives persistent inflammation and tissue damage. The interaction with CXCR6 is especially notable because the CXCL16-CXCR6 axis has been implicated in the retention and positioning of inflammatory immune cells within diseased tissues. In addition, its scavenger receptor activity toward OxLDL suggests a mechanistic link to oxidative stress and macrophage activation, both of which are increasingly recognized in arthritic joints. Thus, CXCL16 is important not only as a mediator of inflammation but also as a potential bridge between altered lipid metabolism, innate immunity, and chronic synovitis.  

Extending from chemotactic recruitment to broader innate recognition and clearance functions, COLEC12 may also be relevant to arthritis because its functions converge on innate immune recognition, phagocytosis, and the handling of oxidatively modified molecules. Arthritis, especially rheumatoid arthritis, is characterized by chronic activation of innate immune pathways in the synovium, including enhanced scavenger receptor activity, oxidative stress, and persistent recognition of endogenous or microbial danger signals. The capacity of COLEC12 to bind bacteria and yeast suggests a plausible role in host-microbe interactions that may influence inflammatory priming or perpetuation of joint inflammation. Its ability to internalize oxLDL is particularly noteworthy, as oxidative modification of lipids and proteins is a common feature of inflamed arthritic tissues and may contribute to endothelial activation, macrophage dysfunction, and amplification of inflammatory cascades. Furthermore, the broad carbohydrate-binding profile of COLEC12 supports a role in pattern recognition and clearance processes, which may affect synovial immune homeostasis. Although the connection to arthritis is likely indirect compared with classical inflammatory mediators, COLEC12 stands out as a plausible contributor to the innate immune and oxidative components of disease pathogenesis.  

In a related manner, MARCO further emphasizes the potential importance of innate immune sensing within this pathway. MARCO is of interest in arthritis because it is a canonical pattern recognition receptor of the innate immune system, and innate immune activation is a major driver of synovial inflammation. Its capacity to bind both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria supports a role in sensing microbial products or structurally related endogenous ligands, which may be relevant to theories linking microbial triggers, dysbiosis, or molecular mimicry to arthritis onset and exacerbation. In macrophage-rich environments such as the inflamed synovium, receptors like MARCO may influence phagocytosis, cytokine production, and polarization states that determine whether inflammation resolves or becomes chronic. The ability to bind unopsonized particles further suggests a role in nonclassical clearance pathways, potentially affecting the removal of debris generated during joint tissue injury. While MARCO is not a classic arthritis biomarker, its functions align closely with mechanisms of macrophage activation and innate immune surveillance that are central to inflammatory joint disease.[[237]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7867067)   

Finally, compared with the more inflammation-centered proteins discussed above, FOLR1 appears to have a more indirect but still potentially relevant connection to arthritis. FOLR1 is less directly connected to arthritis pathogenesis than CXCL16, COLEC12, or MARCO, but it remains potentially relevant because folate metabolism is closely linked to cellular proliferation and to therapeutic mechanisms in inflammatory arthritis. The importance of folate transport for normal cell proliferation suggests that FOLR1 could influence the behavior of rapidly dividing cells, including activated immune cells or hyperplastic synovial fibroblasts in inflammatory joint disease. Most notably, folate pathways are clinically significant in rheumatoid arthritis because antifolate therapy, particularly methotrexate, is a cornerstone of treatment. Although the provided functional description does not directly establish FOLR1 as a mediator of arthritis, its role in folate and folate-analog uptake makes it biologically relevant to drug response, tissue folate homeostasis, and potentially to the metabolic demands of chronic inflammation. Therefore, FOLR1 is best viewed as a protein with translational relevance to arthritis therapeutics rather than as a primary inflammatory driver.[[238]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1894617) [[239]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10508523) [[240]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12854656) [[241]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15259034) [[242]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17286298) [[243]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15703271)

### osteoblast differentiation (GO:0001649) 

Osteoblast differentiation is the developmental and functional program through which mesenchymal progenitor cells acquire the molecular, metabolic, and phenotypic features of bone-forming osteoblasts. This process is essential for skeletal development, physiological bone remodeling, repair of microdamage, and restoration of bone after inflammatory injury. It is governed by a tightly coordinated network of transcription factors, signaling pathways, and microenvironmental cues, including runt-related transcription factor 2, osterix, bone morphogenetic protein signaling, wingless-related integration site signaling, calcium signaling, autophagy, mitochondrial quality control, and epigenetic regulation. In healthy tissue, osteoblast differentiation sustains bone matrix production and mineralization and counterbalances bone resorption by osteoclasts. In inflammatory settings, however, this pathway appears to be highly sensitive to suppression by cytokines, immune cells, oxidative stress, and inflammasome activation. The publications provided suggest that osteoblast differentiation is not merely a background bone biology process in arthritis, but rather a central pathogenic node linking inflammation to structural damage, failed bone repair, altered subchondral remodeling, and disease-specific skeletal phenotypes across rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis.  

Building on this biological framework, the collected literature further indicates that dysregulation of osteoblast differentiation may be a major mechanism through which arthritis contributes to bone pathology, although the direction and consequences of this dysregulation appear to differ by disease context. In rheumatoid arthritis, the dominant pattern is suppression of osteoblast differentiation, which contributes to focal erosions, systemic bone loss, and defective repair. A key study demonstrated that bone marrow B cells enriched near osteocalcin-positive osteoblasts in experimental and human rheumatoid arthritis produce chemokine ligand 3 and tumor necrosis factor, thereby inhibiting osteoblast differentiation through extracellular signal-regulated kinase and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells signaling; neutralization of these mediators or B cell depletion restored osteoblast function and reduced bone erosion, directly linking immune cell activity to impaired bone formation in arthritis [[244]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30510188). Consistent with this inflammatory suppression model, tumor necrosis factor alpha inhibits osteoblast differentiation by repressing special AT-rich sequence-binding protein 2 through nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells and mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, while also antagonizing bone morphogenetic protein signaling, providing a mechanistic explanation for how inflammatory cytokines block osteoblast maturation [[245]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29435145). Additional evidence indicates that inflammasome activation may further amplify this defect: in rheumatoid arthritis fracture models, nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-like receptor family pyrin domain containing 3 inflammasome activity suppresses osteogenic differentiation through ras homolog family member A and ras-related C3 botulinum toxin substrate 1, interleukin 1 beta, and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells signaling, delaying bone repair, whereas pharmacologic inhibition rescues bone formation [[246]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40822518). Epigenetic control is also implicated, as enhancer of zeste homolog 2 represses osteoblast differentiation and worsens arthritis-induced bone destruction through trimethylation of histone H3 lysine 27 at the N-myc downstream regulated gene 2 locus, and separate work further links enhancer of zeste homolog 2 to ferroptosis-mediated osteoblast-osteoclast imbalance in rheumatoid arthritis [[247]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35581496) [[248]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39353382). Therapeutically, several studies support the possibility that restoring osteoblast differentiation may mitigate arthritis-associated bone damage: acetyl-11-keto-beta-boswellic acid counteracts tumor necrosis factor alpha and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells mediated inhibition of osteoblast differentiation, interleukin 3 priming protects pre-osteoblasts from tumor necrosis factor alpha-induced suppression by preserving beta-catenin signaling, and specnuezhenide promotes osteoblastogenesis in inflammatory conditions through kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 signaling and reduction of oxidative stress [[249]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29927820) [[250]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40624526) [[251]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41045622). In osteoarthritis, the relationship appears more complex because abnormal osteoblast differentiation contributes to subchondral bone sclerosis rather than erosive bone loss. Interleukin 26 suppresses osteoblast differentiation in osteoarthritis through cyclooxygenase 2 and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells pathways, indicating that inflammatory inhibition of osteoblast maturation may also occur in degenerative arthritis [[252]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40093804). However, another study found that salt-inducible kinase 1 acts as a brake on osteogenic differentiation in bone marrow stromal cells and that its downregulation is associated with excessive osteogenesis, subchondral osteosclerosis, and cartilage damage, suggesting that in osteoarthritis both insufficient and excessive osteoblast differentiation can be pathogenic depending on anatomical site and disease stage [[253]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39169784). Disease-specific remodeling patterns are also evident in other arthritides: in ankylosing spondylitis, micro ribonucleic acid 96 promotes osteoblast differentiation and bone formation by targeting sclerostin and activating wingless-related integration site signaling, consistent with the pathological new bone formation that characterizes this disease [[254]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31111563). Moreover, exosomal micro ribonucleic acid 486-5p derived from rheumatoid arthritis fibroblast-like synoviocytes promotes osteoblast differentiation through transducer of ERBB2 one and bone morphogenetic protein and mothers against decapentaplegic homolog signaling, showing that even within rheumatoid arthritis there are compensatory tissue-derived signals attempting to restore osteoblast activity [[255]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32406432). Taken together, these studies suggest that osteoblast differentiation is a central interface between inflammation, immunity, bone remodeling, and structural outcome in arthritis: suppression of this pathway drives erosions and failed repair in rheumatoid arthritis, dysregulated or excessive activation contributes to subchondral sclerosis in osteoarthritis, and enhanced activation underlies aberrant bone formation in ankylosing spondylitis.[[244]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30510188) [[245]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29435145) [[246]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40822518) [[247]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35581496) [[248]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39353382) [[249]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29927820) [[250]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40624526) [[251]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41045622) [[252]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40093804) [[253]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39169784) [[254]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31111563) [[255]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32406432) [[256]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33774802) [[145]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37222927) 

Against this literature background, the enrichment result in the present dataset appears biologically consistent with the broader disease framework. There were 14 arthritis-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of osteoblast differentiation, a developmental and functional program that governs the conversion of mesenchymal progenitor cells into bone-forming osteoblasts and thereby regulates bone matrix production, mineralization, skeletal remodeling, and post-inflammatory bone repair. In the context of arthritis, the enrichment of 14 proteins in this pathway is biologically notable because osteoblast differentiation sits at the interface between inflammation and structural outcome, linking cytokine-driven suppression, oxidative stress, inflammasome activity, altered subchondral remodeling, failed repair responses, and disease-specific skeletal manifestations across rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis. This enrichment therefore supports the interpretation that impaired osteoblast maturation and function are not secondary background events, but rather quantitatively represented components of arthritis pathogenesis within the present protein set.

To further contextualize these 14 proteins, we include the protein-protein interaction network visualization below, together with the link to the Search Tool for the Retrieval of Interacting Genes and Proteins webpage for direct network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/467c9452-400f-4c7b-a6ab-7621f63ae307.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=E328845E134D11E8)

Following this network-level overview, the significant proteins identified in the functional enrichment analysis are discussed individually below. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

SPP1 is among the most arthritis-relevant proteins in this list because its annotated function directly places it at the interface of immune activation and inflammatory polarization. By promoting interferon-gamma and interleukin-12 production while suppressing interleukin-10, SPP1 favors a pro-inflammatory, type 1 immune milieu. This is highly pertinent to inflammatory arthritides, including rheumatoid arthritis, where excessive cytokine production, macrophage activation, and pathogenic T-cell responses contribute to synovitis, pannus formation, and progressive joint destruction. In addition, SPP1 is widely recognized as an extracellular matrix-associated cytokine that can influence leukocyte recruitment and tissue remodeling, both central features of arthritic joints. Therefore, the listed function suggests that SPP1 could contribute to arthritis by amplifying inflammatory circuits and sustaining the immune environment that promotes cartilage damage and bone erosion.  

In a related but more bone-focused context, ATRAID stands out because it connects directly to bone biology and osteoclast function, two processes of major importance in arthritis. Its role in promoting osteoblast differentiation and terminal mineralization suggests a potential contribution to bone formation and repair, which is relevant to the abnormal bone remodeling observed across arthritic disorders. Even more notable is its documented role in osteoclasts in mediating the intracellular action of nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates, a drug class used to inhibit bone resorption. This is mechanistically relevant because inflammatory arthritis, particularly rheumatoid arthritis, is characterized by excessive osteoclast activation and focal bone erosion. A protein that regulates osteoclast handling of anti-resorptive agents may influence treatment response or the balance between bone destruction and preservation. Thus, ATRAID is important not only for understanding disease-associated bone remodeling but also for its possible pharmacologic relevance in conditions with arthritis-associated bone loss.[[257]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29745899) 

Shifting from bone cell regulation to extracellular matrix remodeling, TNC is highly relevant to arthritis because it is an extracellular matrix protein with functions in cell migration, integrin signaling, and angiogenesis, all of which are central to synovial pathology. Arthritic joints undergo extensive remodeling of the extracellular matrix, accompanied by fibroblast activation, endothelial cell sprouting, leukocyte infiltration, and invasive pannus formation. The ability of TNC to engage multiple integrins suggests that it may influence adhesion-dependent signaling in synovial fibroblasts, immune cells, and endothelial cells. Its angiogenic activity is particularly important, since neovascularization supports the persistence of chronic synovitis by enabling inflammatory cell trafficking and nutrient delivery to hyperplastic synovial tissue. Accordingly, the listed functions support a plausible role for TNC in promoting the structural and vascular changes that sustain inflammatory arthritis.[[165]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19884327) 

Closely related to this matrix-centered perspective, VCAN is notable in the context of arthritis because it links extracellular matrix organization to cell behavior. Its ability to bind hyaluronic acid is especially relevant to joint biology, as hyaluronic acid is a major constituent of synovial fluid and cartilage-associated matrices. In arthritis, alterations in matrix composition and cell-matrix interactions contribute to synovial expansion, inflammatory cell retention, and impaired tissue mechanics. A molecule such as VCAN, which regulates intercellular signaling and cell motility while structurally connecting cells to the matrix, could participate in the remodeling of the inflamed synovium and in the altered biomechanical environment of the arthritic joint. These functions make VCAN a plausible contributor to both inflammatory persistence and tissue degeneration in arthritis.  

Continuing with matrix-cell communication, ITGA11 is of interest for arthritis because collagen recognition is fundamental to joint tissue homeostasis and pathology. Cartilage, synovium, ligaments, and subchondral bone all contain collagen-rich extracellular matrices, and integrin-mediated interactions with collagen strongly influence fibroblast adhesion, migration, and matrix remodeling. In inflammatory arthritis, activated synovial fibroblasts acquire an invasive phenotype that promotes cartilage destruction and perpetuates inflammation. A collagen receptor such as ITGA11 may therefore be relevant to how stromal cells sense and remodel the joint matrix during disease progression. Although the listed annotation is concise, its implication for matrix-cell communication makes ITGA11 a potentially meaningful mediator of structural damage and fibrotic remodeling in arthritic tissues.  

From the perspective of systemic skeletal regulation, FGF23 is potentially relevant to arthritis primarily through systemic bone and mineral metabolism rather than direct synovial inflammation. Arthritis, particularly chronic inflammatory forms, is frequently associated with altered bone turnover, periarticular osteopenia, and broader skeletal complications. Although the listed function emphasizes Klotho-related anti-aging endocrine effects and insulin/insulin-like growth factor 1 signaling, this axis intersects with pathways that influence skeletal maintenance, tissue repair, and age-associated susceptibility to degenerative joint disease. Therefore, FGF23 may be more indirectly connected to arthritis than proteins such as SPP1, ATRAID, or TNC, but it remains noteworthy because endocrine regulators of mineral metabolism can shape the skeletal context in which arthritic damage occurs.  

Returning more directly to osteoblast biology, SMOC1 merits attention because regulation of osteoblast differentiation is directly relevant to the bone remodeling abnormalities seen in arthritis. Inflammatory arthritis is characterized not only by bone erosion but also by defective repair, while some arthritic conditions additionally exhibit aberrant new bone formation. A protein that influences osteoblast differentiation could therefore affect whether bone is appropriately regenerated or remains structurally compromised in diseased joints. Although the annotation does not directly mention inflammation, its role in skeletal developmental programs and osteoblast biology suggests that SMOC1 could be relevant to the balance between bone destruction and repair in arthritis.  

Extending this theme to coupled tissue remodeling and vascular responses, CRIM1 is a potentially relevant arthritis-associated candidate because it combines regulation of bone morphogenetic protein signaling with effects on angiogenesis. Bone morphogenetic protein pathways are important in cartilage and bone homeostasis, and their dysregulation may influence joint remodeling, osteophyte formation, and repair responses. The role of CRIM1 in capillary formation is also noteworthy, as angiogenesis is a hallmark of inflamed synovium and contributes to chronicity by supporting leukocyte influx and tissue expansion. Thus, while CRIM1 is not as directly linked to arthritis as some other proteins in the list, its functions suggest possible involvement in the vascular and tissue-remodeling components of joint disease.  

Moving from stromal and vascular biology back to innate immune signaling, CLEC5A stands out as an immune receptor capable of driving macrophage pro-inflammatory cytokine production, which is a core mechanism in inflammatory arthritis. Although the annotation is framed in the context of microbial infection, the underlying biology is highly relevant: macrophage activation and TYROBP-dependent signaling are central to the cytokine networks that sustain synovitis and promote tissue damage. Receptors that amplify innate immune activation can contribute to arthritis either by responding to infectious triggers in reactive forms of arthritis or by participating more broadly in sterile inflammatory signaling within the joint. Therefore, CLEC5A is noteworthy as a mechanistic link to macrophage-driven inflammation, even though the cited evidence specifically concerns dengue virus recognition.[[120]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18496526) [[121]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21566123) 

Finally, in a comparatively more indirect regulatory context, YAP1 is less directly connected to arthritis based on the listed annotation, but it remains of possible interest because YAP-family transcriptional co-regulators are broadly involved in mechanotransduction, cell proliferation, and tissue remodeling. In the arthritic joint, altered mechanical stress, synovial hyperplasia, and aberrant repair responses are all biologic contexts in which YAP1-related signaling may become relevant. The specific function provided here, activation of the ERBB4 C-terminal fragment, suggests participation in growth-regulatory signaling networks that could influence stromal cell behavior. However, compared with proteins involved in cytokine signaling, extracellular matrix interactions, or osteoclast and osteoblast biology, the connection of YAP1 to arthritis is more indirect on the basis of the current annotation.
